posts.title: Building a cosy block puzzle with Claude
posts.excerpt: Gridlock Garden is a relaxing 8×8 block puzzle I made with Claude. This time I focused on getting the rules right and keeping them tested before adding the polish.
body: Gridlock Garden is a cosy block-placement puzzle: drag pastel garden tiles onto an 8×8 bed, fill whole rows or columns, and watch them bloom away in a burst of petals. It's built with Phaser 3, TypeScript, Vite and Vitest, and I made it with Claude.
After building Apex Club with ChatGPT Astra, I wanted to try a different AI agent on a different kind of game. A puzzle game lives or dies by its rules, so I kept the focus there.

- Rules first, graphics second. Everything about placing pieces, clearing lines, scoring, combos and game over is plain TypeScript with no Phaser code, so it can be tested without a browser. Phaser just animates what the rules say happened.
- 71 unit tests, including one that plays a full game from start to finish with a seeded random generator, so it gives the same result every run.
- No image or sound files. Tiles, petals and the board are drawn in code, and the sound effects are generated with the Web Audio API.

- Then the polish: one undo per game (it can even rescue a game that just ended), a hint button, phone vibration when you place and clear, four themes including a dark Night Garden, and a stats screen showing your last 10 scores.
What I learned: keeping the rules separate and tested made it easy to keep adding features like undo and stats without worrying about breaking the scoring.
It works on desktop and phone, and your best score is saved in your browser. Give it a go.

posts.title: Adding a safe demo mode to a client app
posts.excerpt: My Medicine Tracker is a private client app with no login. Here's how I made a public demo anyone can try, without ever touching the real data.
body: Medicine Tracker is a phone-first app I built for a client who tracks daily medicine for their pets. It has no login on purpose: one client, one database, open the app and tick the dose. That's great for the client, but it means I can't just share the link in my portfolio.
So I added a demo mode. One environment variable (NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO_MODE=1) on a separate Vercel project turns the same code into a safe public demo:
- Every visitor starts with the same made-up pets (Milo, Coco and Oreo) and a few weeks of sample history.
- Changes are saved in the visitor's own browser cookie, so nobody sees anyone else's edits. A Reset demo button brings the sample data back.
- The database client refuses to start in demo mode, so it can't reach Supabase even by mistake, and push notifications are switched off.
What I learned: making a demo safe is a design decision, not an afterthought. Failing closed (the database simply won't start) is much easier to trust than remembering to hide things one by one.

posts.title: Building a racing game with ChatGPT Astra
posts.excerpt: Apex Club is a top-down rally racer made with an AI coding agent. My job shifted from typing code to describing, testing and steering.
body: Apex Club is a top-down rally racer: drive the orange car around Pinecrest Circuit and beat three computer drivers over three laps. It's built with Phaser, TypeScript and Vite, and I made it with ChatGPT Astra.
Working with an AI agent changed what my job was. Instead of writing every line, I spent my time describing how the game should feel, playing each build, and pointing out what was off.
- Clear, specific requests worked far better than vague ones. "The car should slide a little in corners" beats "make it feel better".
- Testing is still on me. Keyboard and touch controls, the lap counter and saving the best lap all needed real play-testing.
- Knowing the code matters. When something broke, being able to read the TypeScript made fixing it much faster.
It runs in the browser on desktop and phone, so give it a try and see if you can beat my best lap.

posts.title: Redesigning my portfolio from scratch
posts.excerpt: My old site had a wall of text, placeholder projects and nothing to click. Here's what I changed so visitors can see and try my work in seconds.

gallery.caption: First screen: a long About Me paragraph before, a clear intro and two actions after.
Projects: grey "Project 1, 2, 3" placeholders before, real games you can play after.

body: My first portfolio did the job of existing, but not much more. It opened with a long About Me paragraph, the projects were placeholders with grey boxes, and there was nothing a visitor could actually try.
So I rebuilt it with one rule: show the work, don't describe it.
- A short intro at the top says who I am and what I do in two lines, with buttons straight to my games and posts.
- Real projects replaced the placeholders. Every game has a cover and a Play now button, and every web app shows real phone screenshots.
- Games and Projects sit in swipeable sliders, so the page stays short and works well on phones.
- Experience is split into collapsible jobs instead of long paragraphs.
- A new Posts section, the one you're reading, shares build logs and what I'm working on now.
It's plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the content in JSON files, so adding a new project or post is just editing one file.

posts.title: Shipped the Wonderland party mini-game
posts.excerpt: A browser mini-game themed on Alice in Wonderland, built for a group activity. Players try to place the item without looking at the character.
body: A browser mini-game themed on Alice in Wonderland, built for a school group activity. One player places the missing piece without looking at the screen while the team shouts directions.
Built with HTML5 Canvas and plain JavaScript, so it runs on any laptop or projector without installing anything.
